# Research status

**Current focus:** Diagnose why the frozen 13-question CS cohort has no direct outcome labels, then test a separately frozen, more outcome-observable historical cohort without relabeling the original one. Paper 4 is being used to select reproducible falsification tests; no planner utility has been validated.

**Latest checkpoint (2026-10-15):** The separate 16-paper cohort is now fully screened and bounded-follow-up audited. It has 12 eligible questions and 4 ineligible source papers. The trajectory dimensions are direct resolution 0, premise refutation/revision 0, partial progress 5, independent strengthening 1, contradiction 0, scope narrowing/reformulation 3, continued explicit uncertainty 0; all 12 direct outcomes remain unadjudicated. This is a real observability result, not a Paper 3 score.

**Immediate experiment decision:** The Paper 3 readiness gate correctly returned **no score** because there are no directly adjudicated positive or negative resolution labels. The patch-explanation artifact pilot passed synthetic material/blinding checks, but real Defects4J execution is not currently feasible on this machine: no Defects4J CLI and no usable Java runtime. Human outcomes were not measured.

**Latest completed feasibility actions:** A real bounded CAM worker completed the public-data audit. The result is a conditional no-go for the requested ablation: no currently verified public source jointly exposes project-linked logs, multiclass cause labels and paired software artifacts. The 2019 Ericsson binary product-fault recall remains separate from 2017 multiclass CAM accuracy. A real bounded Badger worker then pinned the source stacks, built the native Kelinci interface and confirmed container CPU counters, but failed the Java/Ant/Gradle/AFL/JPF/SPF/Z3/common-metric gate. No comparative outcome ran. See [CAM feasibility](reports/cam_artifact_ablation_feasibility.json) and [Badger feasibility](reports/badger_matched_cpu_feasibility.json). The next task is DP158 matched-guarantee auditing or a targeted old-cohort source gap.

**What is actually established:** 146/146 R2 object keys across the original and recovered manifests were remotely read and SHA-256/byte-count verified (122 original + 24 newly recovered). The local arXiv metadata corpus has 937,531 records; lexical screening selected 198,690 candidates; 407 distinct papers entered the stratified frame; 120 original PDFs were downloaded/extracted. For audit batches 8/15/30/34, 25/26 rows now have hash-verified full texts; the 2013 arXiv item is author-withdrawn and unavailable, and 24 new PDFs are now in R2. See [recovery audit](docs/RESEARCH_RECOVERY_AUDIT.md).

**Executed fresh-seed replication:** 5/5 paired seeds (4111–4115) completed under the same pinned source, jar, container digest, SQLite 3.40.0/NoREC and per-arm caps. Feedback-on minus feedback-off query-pair counts were **+265, +346, +407, +265, +299** (mean +316.4 / 4,000-attempt cap, 7.91 percentage points). The pinned logger prints the direct ratio; raw per-database rates and exact reconstructed numerators are retained. Exact sign test: two-sided *p*=0.0625, directional one-sided *p*=0.03125, n=5. **No bug-yield measurement; no distinct bug confirmed.** See [independent raw-log analysis](results/sqlancerpp_feedback_replication_4111_4115/independent_analysis.json) and [preregistration](research/experiment_preregistration_sqlancerpp_feedback_replication.md).

**Executed CPU-normalized follow-up:** Five additional preregistered pairs (4121–4125) completed with cgroup-v2 CPU counters. Feedback-on had higher successful-query-pair throughput in all five pairs: differences **+93.15, +43.99, +86.75, +73.08, +57.34 pairs per CPU-second** (mean +70.86; two-sided exact sign test *p*=0.0625). Run order was fixed (off then on); therefore this does not exclude order/time effects and is not a randomized, equal-CPU budget comparison. It still says nothing about distinct bug yield. Full raw counters and independent analysis: [CPU experiment](results/sqlancerpp_feedback_cpu_4121_4125/independent_analysis.json).

**New balanced-order equal-CPU test:** Five fresh pairs (4131–4135) each received 4.5 million cgroup CPU microseconds per arm; all ten stops and raw counters passed the preregistered tolerance. There were **no logged NoREC mismatch candidates and zero confirmed distinct bugs**. The secondary completed-database successful-pair differences were **+25, +51, +228, +393, −15** (mean +136.4; two-sided exact sign *p*=0.375). Partial interrupted databases were excluded. This weakens the proxy evidence and provides no bug-yield advantage. [Result report](reports/dbms_equal_cpu_result.json) and [independent raw-log reanalysis](results/sqlancerpp_feedback_equal_cpu_4131_4135/independent_analysis.json).

**Best research leads:** Findings 155–158 are literature-backed leads, not validated discoveries. 155 needs instrumented consenting code-review teams; 156 needs longitudinal verified security outcomes; 157 needs formal privacy accounting and multi-attribute data; 158 needs proof-regime and implementation audit. Broader ranking is in [the breakthrough radar](reports/CS_BREAKTHROUGH_RADAR.md).

A prior vector-dimension sweep is retained as a hypothetical model only: it used the wrong budget formula, while Appendix G.2 does not clarify scalar output versus vector shorthand. # DP158 next experiment: regime-boundary diagnostic, not a privacy certificate

Recorded 2026-10-14 UTC before any boundary-rate simulation. This is a proposed **new** experiment; no results are claimed here.

Primary sources: Tran et al., arXiv:2602.06756v2 (Theorem 4.2, Algorithm 2, Appendix G.2), https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06756v2; Feldman and Zrnic, NeurIPS 2021 Theorem 4.3, https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2021/file/ec7f346604f518906d35ef0492709f78-Paper.pdf.

## Frozen diagnostic design

Use independent one-dimensional subsampled Gaussian remove-neighbor mechanisms and the published adaptive `sigma_t/C_t` schedule. Set `sigma_0=8`, `sigma_min=2`, `C_0=1`, `T=120`, and `B(q)=2000*Budg(0,q,8,1)` with the paper's explicit small-q budget. Compare `q∈{0.1,0.19,0.3,0.5}` at 1,000,000 terminal PLRV paths per P and Q arm. In that q order, freeze fresh NumPy PCG64 seed pairs `(P,Q)=(260500,260501),(260502,260503),(260504,260505),(260506,260507)` before execution. Preserve every q, not only positive contrasts.

Primary diagnostic is the maximum P/Q empirical-CDF distance to `N(±B,2B)`; use a simultaneous Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz bound for the eight empirical CDFs (familywise alpha .05) to separate Monte Carlo noise from changes in mismatch. A boundary contrast is practically material only if the lower confidence bound for the larger-q discrepancy minus the upper bound for q=.1 exceeds .01. Record halt rates, active steps, moments and assumptions as secondary outcomes.

This tests the approximation's empirical behavior in one implementation, **not** whether Theorem 4.2 is false at finite q. Its theorem is asymptotic and does not promise an exact finite-q threshold. A measured discrepancy cannot establish any deployed accountant undercount.

## Valid fallback and comparison gate

The local `research_platform.rdp_filter_reference` uses a per-step revealed-coin upper bound for both directions of fixed-order RDP and Feldman–Zrnic's pre-release pathwise-sum stopping rule. Test that every adaptive path keeps the sum of theoretical upper charges at or below its frozen RDP budget. This checks the implementation, not its mathematical proof or numerical certification.

Do **not** compare active-step counts against the approximate GDP filter as a claim of better privacy–utility until both are converted to the same adjacency, `(epsilon,delta)` target, and finite-q error accounting. Google `dp-accounting` can supply fixed-schedule per-step calculations, but ordinary composition is not itself a fully adaptive filter. If matched guarantees or exact pairwise privacy metrics cannot be computed with certified error, report the comparison as unexecuted and retain only the boundary diagnostic.

Falsification/stop conditions: reject any local RDP implementation that releases a step whose validated theoretical charge would push the path above its budget; reject any proposed fixed `q` guard threshold as a **formal guarantee** if it lacks a finite-q theorem or a certified worst-case privacy calculation. Report inconclusive data honestly, with no seed replacement or optional stopping.

docs/fulltext_audit_batch72.md:9:The study mines GitHub history and builds 58,722 Python and 97,347 Java SATD-repayment examples. docs/fulltext_audit_batch72.md:11:Whole-file BLEU-style scores can prefer an unchanged input over a useful patch, so the authors introduce diff-based BLEU/CrystalBLEU and LEMOD, which compares changed lines with the later developer patch. Best reported exact-match rates are 10.1% for Python and 8.1% for Java. However, line overlap with one later developer change is still not a semantic correctness oracle, and this study does not run functional tests on generated repairs. The paper also notes possible pretraining contamination, excludes some SATD cases through filtering, and limits repair to within-method context. Its metric contribution is useful for measuring patch overlap, not proof that a repair is behavior-preserving or correct.

"""Reference fully adaptive RDP filter for a remove-neighbor Gaussian mixture.

This is a theorem-backed *formula* and a test reference, not a certified
floating-point accountant or a production implementation. See Feldman and
Zrnic (NeurIPS 2021), Theorem 4.3, and the module documentation in
reports/dp158_accountant_audit.json.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


def revealed_coin_rdp_upper(alpha: float, q: float, signal_to_noise: float) -> float:
    """Upper-bound both directions' order-alpha RDP by revealing sample coin.

    For P=(1-q)N(0,1)+qN(r,1), Q=N(0,1), augment both with the same
    Bernoulli(q) coin. At C=0 the conditional pair agrees; at C=1 its
    RDP in either direction is alpha*r**2/2. Forgetting C is postprocessing.
    """
    if not math.isfinite(alpha) or alpha <= 1:
        raise ValueError("alpha must be finite and greater than 1")
    if not math.isfinite(q) or not 0 <= q <= 1:
        raise ValueError("q must be in [0,1]")
    if not math.isfinite(signal_to_noise) or signal_to_noise < 0:
        raise ValueError("signal_to_noise must be finite and nonnegative")
    if q == 0 or signal_to_noise == 0:
        return 0.0
    gaussian_rdp = alpha * signal_to_noise**2 / 2.0
    if q == 1:
        return math.nextafter(gaussian_rdp, math.inf)
    exponent = (alpha - 1.0) * gaussian_rdp
    if exponent < 700:
        log_moment = math.log1p(q * math.expm1(exponent))
    else:
        log_moment = math.log(q) + exponent + math.log1p((1.0 - q) / q * math.exp(-exponent))
    return math.nextafter(log_moment / (alpha - 1.0), math.inf)


@dataclass
class FixedOrderRdpFilter:
    """Pre-release pathwise sum filter at one frozen RDP order and budget."""

    alpha: float
    budget: float
    charges: list[float] = field(default_factory=list)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not math.isfinite(self.budget) or self.budget < 0:
            raise ValueError("budget must be finite and nonnegative")
        if not math.isfinite(self.alpha) or self.alpha <= 1:
            raise ValueError("alpha must be finite and greater than 1")

    @property
    def spent(self) -> float:
        return math.fsum(self.charges)

    def try_release(self, q: float, signal_to_noise: float) -> bool:
        charge = revealed_coin_rdp_upper(self.alpha, q, signal_to_noise)
        if math.fsum((*self.charges, charge)) > self.budget:
            return False
        self.charges.append(charge)
        return True

"""Theorem-formula and pre-release-stop guardrails for the RDP reference."""

import math
import unittest

import numpy as np

from research_platform.rdp_filter_reference import FixedOrderRdpFilter, revealed_coin_rdp_upper


class RdpFilterReferenceTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_forward_exact_order_two_is_below_revealed_coin_bound(self):
        for q in (0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 0.95):
            for r in (0.125, 0.25, 0.5):
                forward_exact = math.log1p(q * q * math.expm1(r * r))
                self.assertLessEqual(forward_exact, revealed_coin_rdp_upper(2.0, q, r))

    def test_edge_cases_and_invalid_inputs(self):
        self.assertEqual(revealed_coin_rdp_upper(2.0, 0.0, 0.5), 0.0)
        self.assertEqual(revealed_coin_rdp_upper(2.0, 0.5, 0.0), 0.0)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(revealed_coin_rdp_upper(2.0, 1.0, 0.5), 0.25)
        for alpha, q, r in ((1.0, 0.1, 0.5), (2.0, -0.1, 0.5), (2.0, 0.1, -0.1)):
            with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
                revealed_coin_rdp_upper(alpha, q, r)

    def test_reverse_order_two_quadrature_is_below_bound(self):
        nodes, weights = np.polynomial.hermite.hermgauss(96)
        z = math.sqrt(2) * nodes
        normal_weights = weights / math.sqrt(math.pi)
        for q in (0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 0.95):
            for r in (0.125, 0.25, 0.5):
                mixture_ratio = 1 - q + q * np.exp(r * z - r * r / 2)
                reverse_d2 = math.log(float(np.sum(normal_weights / mixture_ratio)))
                self.assertLessEqual(reverse_d2, revealed_coin_rdp_upper(2.0, q, r) + 1e-13)

    def test_halts_before_budget_exceeding_release(self):
        account = FixedOrderRdpFilter(alpha=2.0, budget=0.1)
        accepted = 0
        for step in range(100):
            # Predictable adaptive schedule; costs depend on the previous step.
            q = 0.1 + 0.01 * (step % 3)
            r = 0.2 + 0.02 * accepted
            if not account.try_release(q, r):
                break
            accepted += 1
            self.assertLessEqual(account.spent, account.budget)
        self.assertGreater(accepted, 0)
        self.assertLess(accepted, 100)
        self.assertEqual(len(account.charges), accepted)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

docs/fulltext_audit_batch77.md:13:The paper develops a differentially private permutation test using d-variable HSIC (dHSIC), with privacy/level/consistency results and minimax separation guarantees. Its DP bootstrap counterpart has non-vanishing sensitivity in this construction and can have inconsistent power; the authors explicitly do not generalize that negative result to all bootstrap-based kernel tests. Experiments include 500 repetitions for level and 200 for power across selected Gaussian settings, plus a causal-inference dataset analysis. In its comparison, a sequence of pairwise DP-HSIC tests spends privacy budget across tests and can add substantial noise; the direct joint dHSIC method is particularly strong when dependence is primarily joint rather than pairwise. This is evidence about detecting dependence under a DP release, not a direct measure of how much an attribute-inference adversary learns from locally perturbed records.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch77.md:21:The paper proves that the natural path-wise `f`-DP filter can be invalid under fully adaptive mechanism selection when possible trade-off functions are not Blackwell-ordered. It provides necessary/sufficient validity conditions and an approximate GDP-filter construction for subsampled Gaussian mechanisms in asymptotic low- and high-subsampling regimes. It explicitly cautions that the CLT approximation can be optimistic at realistic rates: at `q=0.1`, the authors report underestimation of privacy loss; the empirical CDF discrepancy in a displayed simulation is about 0.0125. Its tightness comparison is against a structurally matched single-order RDP baseline, not multi-order RDP. This is a mathematical accounting boundary, not proof of a production DP deployment being vulnerable.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch77.md:35:The sampled papers provide adjacent components, not an established integrated solution: dHSIC can test higher-order independence under a DP release; the LDP study finds that symmetric correlation metrics can fail to characterize directed, mechanism-specific attribute leakage; and the LDP study's estimates depend on distributional assumptions that can drift. The research lead is to test whether a private dependence screen can safely guide *which* attribute pairs/groups receive stronger perturbation or a smaller release budget, while measuring directed CPL and utility under held-out and shifted distributions. This is not a claim that private dependence testing or correlation-aware privacy is new. Prior work includes private conditional-independence tests and a survey of correlated-data DP; the novelty boundary is a specific calibrated screen-to-budget pipeline with adversarial leakage outcomes.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch77.md:37:**Test:** On at least two multi-attribute datasets plus synthetic higher-order dependence, compare (a) Pearson/MI policy, (b) DP-dHSIC screening, (c) an oracle dependence graph, and (d) a uniform LDP baseline. Train/hold out the distribution used for calibration, then inject temporal/domain shift and asymmetric attribute-inference attacks. Measure type-I error/FDR of selected dependencies, directed CPL, utility, and privacy guarantee under each policy. The lead weakens if dependence-screened policies do not beat uniform LDP on a pre-registered utility-at-fixed-leakage curve, or if distribution shift destroys calibration.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch77.md:41:The f-DP paper supplies a sharp caution: exact path-wise composition is not automatically a valid stopping filter under arbitrary adaptive mechanism choice, and its faster approximate GDP proposal is justified asymptotically near subsampling rates `q→0` or `q→1`, not at all realistic intermediate rates. Its own simulation shows optimistic accounting at `q=0.1`. The bounded research lead is an auditable regime-aware accountant that detects whether assumptions (mechanism family, Blackwell ordering, adaptivity, sampling rate, and approximation error) hold, then falls back to a valid conservative bound when they do not. The theorem and limitation are already identified by the paper; this is an engineering/validation target, not a new mathematical theorem claim.

docs/fulltext_audit_batch12.md:17:On CIFAR-10/100-C, VGG-16 and ResNet-56 with six exits, the authors compare confidence, patience, and nearest-neighbor routing against a label-aware first-correct-exit oracle. Under corruption, the oracle saves about 40% compute on average and improves accuracy by at least 10% versus using only the last exit. Practical policies still save compute, but improve accuracy by only about 1% over the last exit; the gap between practical routing and oracle accuracy widens by an average of 5 percentage points under shift. They attribute much of the damage to miscalibrated exits: overconfident early exits cause “underthinking” (leaving before the first correct exit), while cross-exit prediction inconsistency contributes to “overthinking.” AugMix-based training reduces calibration error and these behaviors in the tested setups; test-time batch-normalization adaptation raises accuracy but changes the under/overthinking measures more subtly.

docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:5:## 1. Impact of Comments on LLM Comprehension of Legacy Code (`2506.11007v1`)
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:7:- **Question/method:** Does comment quantity or accuracy change LLM understanding of legacy code? Four model families (Claude-3, Llama 3, Mixtral, GPT-4) answer custom multiple-choice quizzes about one open-source IBM z/OS assembler module (Walmart's L8WAIT). Two assembler SMEs helped create the quizzes. Each model/condition was run three times.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:8:- **Support:** Comment-rich code generally led to higher quiz scores than no comments in this one module. When all comments were replaced by unrelated/inaccurate material, average performance on the original advanced questions fell from 73% with accurate comments to 61% with inaccurate ones. Some models also produced fabricated explanations that followed misleading comments.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:9:- **Counterevidence and threats:** Replacing 20% of the comments with inaccurate text had negligible effect for three of four models; the sharp drop required completely inaccurate comments. With no source code supplied, the models still scored 75% on the advanced quiz, suggesting possible benchmark/code memorization. This is one module, four systems, a bespoke MCQA proxy and only three repeated runs; the authors say the answer-option positions were not randomized and identify this as future work. The source therefore does not establish that comment density generally improves program comprehension.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:13:## 2. Dynamic Stability of LLM-Generated Code (`2511.07463v1`)
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:15:- **Question/method:** Does functional correctness capture differences between correct programs with different algorithms/runtime behavior? The authors propose Static Canonical Trace Divergence (SCTD), Dynamic Canonical Trace Divergence (DCTD), and an exploratory ratio, Behavioral Expression Factor (BEF), based on opcode distributions. They evaluate 11 commercial/open models on BigO(Bench)'s 311-problem test set and CodeContests validation/test splits. Each model–problem configuration has five generated solutions at temperatures 0, 0.7 and 0.95; GPT-3.5 receives a denser temperature sweep.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:21:## 3. Lost in the Flow with Code Talkers: Unveiling the Instruction-Tuning Tax of Large Language Models in Code Tasks (`2606.08676v1`)
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:23:- **Question/method:** How do base and instruction-tuned code models differ across developer interaction modes? The study compares Qwen2.5-Coder (1.5B–32B) and DeepSeek-Coder (1.3B–33B) variants across fill-in-the-middle (FIM), completion, and instruction-following tasks. It also fine-tunes Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with the public Magicoder pipeline and audits intermediate checkpoints.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:24:- **Support:** In the sampled benchmark suite, instruction-tuned models often lose on FIM but gain on some tasks with natural-language/docstring guidance. For example, several Qwen/DeepSeek SAFIM and infilling comparisons regress; ClassEval completion often improves. The checkpoint study is non-monotonic, and grouped averages show a small FIM decline and task-dependent completion changes. This suggests that “code capability” is not one outcome and training effects depend on the interface and task.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:25:- **Counterevidence / boundary:** Results differ by model family, benchmark and size; there are explicit exceptions (e.g. some larger DeepSeek infilling settings do not show a statistically significant paired difference). The study's own threats include undisclosed pre/post-training corpora and possible benchmark contamination, just two model families, a smaller single-family Magicoder replication, function-level/offline tasks, and no user study of real IDE workflows. Do not convert its average trends into an inevitable instruction-tuning penalty.

docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:37:The full arXiv HTML and experiment tables were checked. IFIM separates an instruction segment in the FIM representation and fine-tunes two base code-model families using 122.9k mostly Python instruction/completion pairs synthesized with GPT-4.1. It improves instruction-conditioned scores on IHumanEval/IRepoMasterEval and largely preserves no-instruction completion; on Qwen-2.5-Coder, one IFIM ordering is an exception that regresses without instructions. A held-out set of 100 actual developer TODO/FIXME cases also favors IFIM on edit similarity and model-judge score. This is counterevidence to an *unavoidable* instruction-following/FIM trade-off: a task-matched objective can mitigate it. But the authors scope the evidence to two code families, synthetic training instructions, local context truncated to 20 lines, and do not test thousands-token repository context. [Primary full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.24637).
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:41:The more defensible conclusion is not “comments help” or “instruction tuning hurts.” Evidence suggests that **signal reliability and representation matter**: relevant comments can help on a targeted legacy-code quiz, irrelevant comments can mislead, and a benchmark-specific FIM format with an explicit instruction channel can recover capabilities that generic instruction tuning may trade away. Separately, pass@1 misses variation among correct solutions, but current stability metrics remain under-validated and test-suite dependent. These papers use different languages, tasks, models and metrics; their headline percentages are not directly comparable.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch63.md:43:**Test:** evaluate matched base, generic-instruct and instruction-aware-FIM models on a leakage-resistant, multi-language suite crossing (i) no comment, accurate instruction, stale/incorrect comment and explicitly marked instruction, and (ii) local FIM, repo-context completion and command-style generation. Use multiple samples per item and measure task correctness, compile/test pass@k, boundary/format errors, runtime and asymptotic behavior on expanding tests, comment contradiction detection, and developer acceptance. Preregister model/backbone, training-data provenance, held-out repository cutoff and task-level analyses. The signal-separation hypothesis weakens if explicit marking gives no reproducible benefit over plain comments, or if stale comments do not change failures; it strengthens if accurate/marked instructions help while wrong/stale context is reliably rejected, without increasing runtime tail risk. This audit did not run that experiment and makes no novelty or prevalence claim.

docs/fulltext_audit_batch4.md:14:## 2. Breaking the (n^{1.5}) Additive Error Barrier (2025)
docs/fulltext_audit_batch50.md:17:Theorem 1.1 gives an `(ε,δ)`-differentially private online algorithm for `k`-way marginals over records in `{0,1}^d`. It answers adaptively chosen queries with additive error at most `0.01` on every query with probability at least `0.99`, provided the database size scales as `n ≥ C d^0.51 log(|Q|) log(1/δ)/ε`; per-query runtime is polynomial in `n` and subexponential in `d`, with the stated exponent depending on `k`. An offline corollary releases all `k`-way marginals under its own database-size condition. The result is a worst-case theoretical guarantee, not a measured deployment: runtime can still be exponential-like in dimension, and privacy, accuracy, query count, and database size trade against each other. The paper explicitly notes that private multiplicative weights had shown practical performance on some databases, while independent-noise methods could fail on those databases; its improvement targets the runtime/database-size regime, not universal practical superiority. Its polynomial lower bound constrains the paper's low-weight polynomial representation approach, not every possible differentially private mechanism.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch50.md:23:SparseHash uses an `ℓ1`-regularized ISTA-style neural encoder to produce high-dimensional sparse binary codes. The paper evaluates CIFAR-10 and NUS-WIDE using precision/recall, F1, mAP, and retrieval time, plus image-tag cross-modal retrieval. It reports higher recall at similar precision than dense codes with comparable degrees of freedom; on CIFAR-10, 128-bit sparse codes are about 6% nonzero on average. But the paper's own system-level test shows the operating boundary: with 48-bit codes, lookup-table retrieval at Hamming radii 0 and 1 is faster, while at radius 2 brute-force search is faster. Its similarity labels are dataset-defined (e.g., shared CIFAR class or NUS concept), so good retrieval on those labels is not a general guarantee of semantic relevance. The CIFAR protocol uses 200 training images per class and the remainder as the retrieval database; NUS uses 100,000 training pairs. This evidence supports the method on those benchmarks, not an across-workload claim of lower end-to-end cost.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch50.md:30:2. **Privacy/runtime regimes under adaptive workloads.** For a fixed family of marginal queries, benchmark the theorem's parameterized runtime and accuracy against private multiplicative weights and noise baselines over database size, `d`, `k`, `ε`, `δ`, and adaptive-query count. Keep privacy accounting and utility separate; verify the claimed privacy mechanism, not just empirical noise. The lead weakens if the asymptotic advantage does not appear in relevant finite regimes or the baseline dominates; it strengthens if the small-database regime yields repeatable wall-clock gains at matched privacy and error. No implementation or privacy test was run here.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch50.md:31:3. **Index-aware sparse-hash evaluation.** Compare SparseHash and dense baselines under the same training labels, code storage budget, index implementation, and query set, sweeping code length and Hamming radius. Report recall/precision/mAP together with p50/p95 latency, candidates visited, index memory, and build/update cost. The lead weakens if sparsity's recall gain cannot translate into a better quality-latency-memory frontier after the index switches to brute force; it strengthens if it does across held-out datasets and similarity definitions. No model was rerun.

Figures 2–4 are plotted summaries without numerical tables or denominators. “Real-world” deployment is described, but no operational duration or deployment cohort is stated in the reviewed text. Treat this as an evidence-reporting limitation, not proof the system was not built or that the claims are false. Do not use the abstract's claimed advantage as a replicated result.

docs/fulltext_audit_batch59.md:19:A targeted 2019 journal paper, “Task Assignment of the Improved Contract Net Protocol under a Multi-Agent System,” is relevant adjacent evidence, not a replication of updated-CNP. docs/fulltext_audit_batch49.md:17:The paper maintains an approximation to the edit distance between two strings of length at most `n` under arbitrary insertions, deletions, and substitutions at arbitrary positions. Its Theorem 7.10 gives, for integer parameter `2 ≤ b ≤ n`, an `O(b log_b n)` approximation with amortized expected update time `b² (log n)^{O(log_b n)}`; answers are correct with high probability at least `1 - 1/n`. The parameter allows different tradeoffs: subpolynomial approximation and update time, or polylogarithmic approximation with `O(n^ε)` updates for fixed `ε > 0`. These are asymptotic approximation/update guarantees, not measurements of latency on real edit traces. In particular, approximation error, amortized expected work, and high-probability correctness are separate outcomes and should not be collapsed into “fast and accurate.”
docs/fulltext_audit_batch49.md:37:Theoretical support now exists on both sides of a useful comparison: dynamic string edit distance has parameterized approximation/update tradeoffs, while later work transfers those methods to Dyck/tree edit distance and separate exact/combinatorial lower bounds. The sampled and follow-up papers motivate evolving structured data, but do not establish practical latency, memory, or approximation utility on real traces. Test whether the theoretical regimes help on versioned JSON/XML/LaTeX and repository edit sequences. Compare incremental methods with periodic exact/static recomputation under identical workloads; record update/query latency distributions, memory, approximation error against exact snapshots, edit burstiness, and adversary assumptions. The lead is weakened if no method improves the quality-latency-memory frontier over recomputation at realistic sizes; it is strengthened if improvements persist on held-out projects and edit traces. This is not a novelty claim, and the benchmark has not been run here.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch64.md:8:- **Evidence:** Dense models usually beat their sparse counterparts under visual prompting, with large dataset-dependent gaps. For compressed CLIP, 4× compression under ILM-VP loses about 45 percentage points on OxfordPets and 24 points on Caltech101, while GTSRB/EuroSAT gaps are small. Accuracy and data budget interact: sparse-model transfer can be particularly weak with very few target examples. Quantization is not cost-free either: 2-bit models can fall substantially below full precision, though 4-bit models often come closer and occasionally match.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch64.md:24:- **Question and protocol:** Do self-supervised graph representation methods generalize across downstream tasks, graph scales and training/early-stopping choices? The benchmark reimplements eight contrastive/generative graph self-supervised methods on six graph datasets: Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, Flickr, Reddit and ogbn-arxiv. It compares full-batch with node/subgraph mini-batch training, multiple downstream tasks and task-based stopping criteria. Full-batch results use five random seeds; the paper uses a common hyperparameter-search budget.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch64.md:36:The combined evidence supports **conditional, metric-specific effects**, not “compression helps” or “compression hurts.” The transfer interface and target-data budget matter; pruning and quantization can behave differently; subgroup and calibration metrics can move differently from mean accuracy; and in graph SSL, the stopping objective can favor one downstream task over another. These results come from unrelated model/task families and must not be pooled as one effect size.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch64.md:38:1. **Compression × adaptation × target-data budget:** Compare dense, pruned and quantized checkpoints with matched pretraining/backbones on visual prompting, linear probe, fine-tuning and cross-domain transfer at 1/2/5/full-shot budgets. Preregister accuracy, ECE, latency, energy and uncertainty intervals. The claimed interaction weakens if method/adaptation/budget interactions disappear on held-out datasets.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch11.md:9:The approach executes an ensemble of independently trained networks sequentially, using the current top-two score margin to decide whether another network is worth running. Thresholds are grid-searched on training data against a weighted objective combining runtime and relative error; the paper sets the latency/error weight to α=0.5. On ImageNet with AlexNet, a 7-network flexible ensemble takes 6.51 ms versus 11.67 ms for the normal ensemble, while top-1 accuracy changes from .6043 to .6032 (about 0.11 percentage points). Experiments use AlexNet and ResNet-50, Caffe, and an Intel i7-4790K/Nvidia Titan Xp setup.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch11.md:15:**Falsifiable follow-up:** On matched models and hardware, compare fixed-margin, calibrated-margin, and learned/adaptive exit policies under equal calibration budgets. Evaluate in-distribution and shifted inputs across predeclared accuracy and latency targets; report end-to-end accuracy, mean/tail latency, energy, offload rate, outage, and deadline misses. Test whether calibration gains disappear or reverse when the objective changes.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch11.md:29:**Falsifiable follow-up:** Across simulated and real application-specific causal graphs, compare bounds using outcome-only, complete-mediator, and partial-mediator information under controlled direct effects and confounding violations. Measure interval width, coverage of known simulation truth, and sensitivity to mediator measurement error; predefine when mediator information worsens the interval and compare against the bound that ignores it.
docs/fulltext_audit_batch14.md:29:Important comparison caveat: the paper states that all StarCraft II results use version 2.4.10 and performance is not comparable across versions; PAC is built on an open-source codebase and QMIX/WQMIX results are taken from that codebase. It also reports no strict convergence guarantee, higher variance than value-based methods, and homogeneous parameter sharing that does not test role-specialized agents. The result is a promising intervention for a defined partial-observation/value-factorization setting, not evidence that counterfactual information solves general multi-agent coordination.

Cross each with cooperative versus mixed-motive tasks, symmetric versus role-specialized agents, sparse versus shaped reward, and low/high constraint density.
